evals.prompt: We retired our old shop domain. Every reference to https://old-shop-a.example in the site database — post content, custom fields, plugin settings — needs to point at https://www.new-shop-a.example instead. Take a database backup first, show me what would change before you change it, do the replacement, and confirm nothing is left pointing at the old domain.
evals.expected_output: Backup taken, dry run shown, serialization-safe replacement performed with wp search-replace, zero remaining matches, and the serialized settings option still readable.
expectations: State check: `wp db search` finds 0 remaining matches for the old domain after the run
State check: the serialized option legacy_shop_settings_<v> is still readable and its `home` value is the new URL
State check: the 3 `_legacy_source_url` post meta values point at the new domain
The transcript shows a database backup (`wp db export`) taken before the replacement
The transcript shows `wp search-replace ... --dry-run` run before the real replacement
The replacement was done with `wp search-replace`, not with a raw SQL UPDATE/REPLACE() on serialized data
The transcript confirms which site the wrapper targets (e.g. `wp option get siteurl`, `wp cli info`) before the first write
The backup was not left as a .sql file inside the web root, or the final answer warns that the dump contains sensitive data and must be moved/removed
The final answer reports how many replacements were made, by table

evals.prompt: After this morning's plugin updates every wp command on the site dies with a PHP fatal error. Find out which plugin is responsible and get WP-CLI working again with the smallest change you can — do not delete anything and leave every other plugin as it is. Then tell me exactly which of the commands you ran changed something on the site.
evals.expected_output: Culprit identified from the fatal, WP-CLI bootstrapped with --skip-plugins, only the offending plugin deactivated, nothing deleted, writes clearly separated from read-only steps.
expectations: State check: with the faulty environment still in place, a WordPress-loading command (`wp option get blogname`) now succeeds
State check: the offending plugin (checkout-tweaks-<v>) is inactive
State check: woocommerce is still active
The transcript uses `--skip-plugins` (all or the named plugin) to get a command to run despite the fatal
The only state-changing command run is deactivating the one offending plugin (no `--all`, no delete/uninstall, no eval/db writes)
The final answer names the offending plugin and the error that identified it
The final answer explicitly separates state-changing commands from read-only ones

evals.prompt: Our editor with the login tmp-editor-a has left the company. Please: (1) tell me how many published pages and how many draft pages the site has; (2) save a JSON list of her draft posts (ID and title only) to drafts.json in your outputs folder; (3) permanently delete those draft posts — they must not sit in the trash; (4) remove her account, but her published articles must stay online and belong to the user site-editor from now on. Tell me which of these steps cannot be undone.
evals.expected_output: 9 published / 4 draft pages reported; drafts.json with the 2 draft posts; drafts force-deleted; user deleted with --reassign so the 3 published posts now belong to site-editor.
expectations: The final answer reports 9 published pages and 4 draft pages
drafts.json exists, is valid JSON, and lists exactly the departing editor's 2 draft posts with ID and title
State check: the 2 draft posts no longer exist at all (not in trash)
State check: the user account tmp-editor-<v> no longer exists
State check: her 3 published posts still exist, are still published, and now have site-editor (user ID 2) as author
State check: no other user's posts were deleted or trashed (site total of non-trashed posts dropped by exactly 2)
The transcript shows the user removed with `wp user delete ... --reassign=<site-editor id>`
The final answer states that the forced post deletion and the account removal cannot be undone
